title: 为什么有些音乐让人浑身一颤
title_en: Why Music Can Send a Shiver Down Your Spine
summary_zh: 听到某段音乐时脊背发麻、手臂起鸡皮疙瘩，这到底是怎么回事？文章介绍“预期与意外”的解释，也坦白告诉你：为什么偏偏表现为鸡皮疙瘩，科学家至今还没有定论。
body: Almost everyone who loves music can name a passage that does something strange to their body: a shiver running down the spine, a tightening of the scalp, a sudden rash of goosebumps along the arms. What is curious is not that music moves us, but that it does so physically, through a reflex that evolved for coping with cold and fear. Researchers have been studying these chills for some time, and while a convincing picture is beginning to emerge, a good deal remains uncertain. The moments that trigger them tend to share a family resemblance. A voice enters after a long instrumental stretch; the volume swells unexpectedly; a melody leaps higher than the ear was prepared for; a harmony slips sideways into an unfamiliar key. In each case, something departs from what the listener expected, yet departs in a way that still makes sense. This is where prediction seems to matter. Listening to music is not a passive activity: the brain is constantly anticipating what will come next, and being proved slightly wrong in a satisfying way appears to be rewarding in itself. Scans of listeners suggest that the brain's reward systems become active not only at the peak itself but in the moments leading up to it, as though anticipating the thrill were part of the pleasure. Unless a piece first builds an expectation, in other words, its surprise has nothing to push against. Nor does familiarity necessarily spoil the effect; many people report chills at the same moment on the tenth hearing as on the first. Why the response should take the form of goosebumps is harder to say. One suggestion is that intensely emotional sounds resemble the calls that once signalled danger or separation, briefly setting off an ancient alarm. Another is that the reaction is simply a by-product of strong emotional arousal. Neither idea has been settled, and not everyone experiences chills at all, which is itself one of the more intriguing puzzles.

They break the listener's expectations in a way that still makes sense

done without active effort or involvement
expensive

questions.evidence: Listening to music is not a passive activity

title: 记忆不是录像，而是重建
title_en: Memories Are Rebuilt, Not Replayed: A Case for Arguing More Gently
summary_zh: 我们总以为回忆是在“回放录像”，其实大脑每次都在用碎片重新拼一遍。作者认为：记忆大体可靠，但细节最容易出错，而我们吵架吵的恰恰是细节。读完你能学会议论文里让步与反驳的高级句式。
body: Most of us talk about our memories as though they were recordings: we play back a conversation, or insist that we can still see exactly what happened. The metaphor is comforting, but it is misleading, and I think it quietly makes our disagreements worse than they need to be. Remembering, as far as psychologists can tell, is less like pressing play than like rebuilding a scene from scattered materials. The brain keeps fragments, such as a face, a phrase or a feeling, and each time we recall an event, it reassembles them, filling the gaps with what usually happens, what we have learned since and what we now believe. The result feels seamless, which is exactly the problem. A rebuilt memory carries no label showing which parts were filled in, and the act of recalling it can itself reshape what is stored for next time. It follows that vividness and confidence, the very qualities we rely on most, are poor guides to accuracy. None of this means that memory is hopeless. For the broad outline of our lives, it is remarkably dependable, and a person who doubted every recollection would be unable to function, let alone hold an opinion. Critics are right to point out that errors tend to cluster in the details rather than in whether events happened at all. But details are precisely what we argue about: who said what, in which order and in what tone. Unless one of us wrote it down at the time, both versions are reconstructions, and insisting on ours is less a matter of evidence than of pride. The practical lesson is a modest one. Saying "this is how I remember it" instead of "this is what happened" costs nothing, and it leaves room for the other person to be partly right. Treating memory as a reconstruction is not a reason to distrust ourselves; it is a reason to argue a little more gently.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main argument?
options: Memory is so unreliable that we should never trust it
Because memories are rebuilt, we should hold our version of the details less firmly when we disagree
Writing everything down is the only way to avoid arguments
Vivid memories are usually more accurate than ordinary ones
questions.evidence: Treating memory as a reconstruction is not a reason to distrust ourselves; it is a reason to argue a little more gently.

questions.prompt: Which point does the writer accept from critics?

People who doubt their memories argue less

title: 书评：《地壳下的水壶》
title_en: Book Review: The Kettle Under the Crust
summary_zh: 一篇科普书书评（书为虚构）：这本讲火山的书不从灾难写起，而从一锅煮沸的浓汤讲起，清楚解释了岩石会在哪三种地方熔化、为什么有的火山缓缓流淌、有的猛烈爆发。读完你能学会书评“先扬后抑再总结”的写法。
body: Popular books about volcanoes usually open with a catastrophe, and readers could be forgiven for expecting The Kettle Under the Crust to do the same. Instead, its author, a field geologist with a gift for plain explanation, begins in a kitchen, watching a pan of thick soup come slowly to the boil. It is a disarming start, and it sets the tone for a book that is more interested in mechanisms than in disasters. The early chapters are its strongest. Rock deep underground is extremely hot, the author explains, but it is usually kept solid by the enormous pressure above it. To melt it, nature relies on three main tricks. Where two plates pull apart, as along the ocean floor, hot rock rises, the pressure on it falls and part of it melts. Where one plate dives beneath another, it carries water down with it, and that water lowers the melting point of the rock above, much as salt lowers the freezing point of an icy road. And in a few places far from any plate edge, columns of unusually hot rock seem to rise from deep inside the Earth, although exactly how these form is still argued over, a point the book handles with admirable honesty. The middle section, on why some volcanoes ooze while others explode, is equally clear. Sticky, gas-rich magma traps its bubbles until the pressure becomes too great, rather like a shaken bottle of fizzy drink, whereas runnier magma lets the gas escape quietly. The book is less sure-footed when it turns to prediction. The final chapters, while careful not to overpromise, feel thin, and the kitchen metaphor, charming at first, is stretched until it creaks. Unless you are particularly fond of soup, the twentieth comparison to a simmering pan may test your patience. These are minor complaints, however. For curious readers with no background in geology, this is an unusually generous introduction, and it is hard to finish it without wanting to see a volcano for yourself, preferably from a safe distance.

title: 为什么自己挠自己不痒
summary_zh: 别人轻轻一挠你就笑个不停，自己挠却毫无感觉。原来大脑会预测自身动作带来的感觉，并把它“调小音量”。读完你会明白这种预测有多重要，也会知道：人被挠为什么会笑，至今仍没有定论。
body: Try tickling the soles of your own feet and you will almost certainly be disappointed. The same light touch that would have you squirming if someone else delivered it produces, at most, a faint itch. The reason has less to do with the skin than with the brain, which turns out to be a remarkably busy forecaster. Whenever you move, the brain does not simply send instructions to your muscles; it also keeps a copy of those instructions and uses it to predict what the movement will feel like. When the actual sensation arrives, it is compared with the forecast, and anything that matches is turned down, rather like a familiar background noise that you stop noticing. Because your own fingers are following orders you issued yourself, their touch is predicted in almost perfect detail, and the brain has little reason to pay it much attention. A tickle from someone else is a different matter. Its timing, pressure and direction cannot be anticipated precisely, so the signal reaches you at full strength. One way to test the idea is to introduce a gap between the action and the sensation, for instance by having people move a device that strokes their own palm after a short delay or at an unexpected angle. Experiments along these lines suggest that the less the touch matches the prediction, the more ticklish it feels. Being able to dampen self-produced sensations is far from a party trick. Without it, every step, every scratch and every brush of your own hand against your face would compete for attention with genuinely new information from the world outside. Unless the predictable is filtered out, the unpredictable has little chance of standing out. Why being tickled by others should make us laugh, however, remains surprisingly hard to explain, and researchers continue to disagree about what that laughter is for.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why can't you tickle yourself?
options: Your fingers are not sensitive enough
The brain predicts the touch of your own movements and turns it down
Your skin slowly gets used to your own touch
You cannot move your hands quickly enough
questions.evidence: their touch is predicted in almost perfect detail, and the brain has little reason to pay it much attention

questions.prompt: What do the experiments with a delayed device suggest?
options: Any delay makes people less sensitive to touch
Machines can never make people feel ticklish
A touch feels more ticklish the less it matches the brain's prediction
People laugh more when they control the device themselves
questions.evidence: the less the touch matches the prediction, the more ticklish it feels

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say being able to dampen self-produced sensations is "far from a party trick"?
options: Only a few people have this skill
It was first noticed at a party
It helps the brain notice genuinely new information
It makes being tickled more fun
questions.evidence: Unless the predictable is filtered out, the unpredictable has little chance of standing out.

questions.prompt: What does "squirming" mean in "would have you squirming"?
options: running away
twisting your body because of discomfort
shouting angrily
sleeping deeply

expressions.note: have sb doing 表示“使某人一直处于某种状态”：The film had us laughing all night.

expressions.text: has less to do with the skin than with the brain
expressions.meaning: 与其说和皮肤有关，不如说和大脑有关
expressions.note: have less to do with A than with B 用来纠正对原因的误解，论证时很地道。
引出出乎意料的事实：The quiet student turned out to be a brilliant singer.
转折时对比两种情况：Reading English is easy for me; speaking is a different matter.

expressions.meaning: 沿着这个思路的；类似这样的
expressions.note: 指方向相同的做法或想法：We need something along these lines, but cheaper.
far from + 名词/形容词＝远非……；a party trick 指聚会上逗乐的小把戏。

knowledge.quote: Being able to dampen self-produced sensations is far from a party trick.
knowledge.explanation: 动名词短语 Being able to … 作主语，把“能够做某事”这种能力当成名词来讨论，谓语用单数 is。

knowledge.quote: Because your own fingers are following orders you issued yourself, their touch is predicted in almost perfect detail
knowledge.explanation: because 引导原因状语从句放在句首，先交代原因再给结果；从句里 orders you issued yourself 省略了关系词 that。

knowledge.quote: Unless the predictable is filtered out, the unpredictable has little chance of standing out.
knowledge.explanation: unless ＝ if … not：可预测的感觉如果不被过滤掉，新的信号就很难被注意到。the predictable / the unpredictable 是“the + 形容词”，表示一类事物。

speaking: 用 1 分钟解释为什么自己挠自己不痒，并举一个生活中大脑自动忽略熟悉信号的例子（如钟表声、衣服贴在身上的感觉）。用上 turns out to be 和 a different matter。
writing: 用 200–250 词解释一个身体上的小怪现象（如打嗝、腿麻、手指泡水后起皱），写清目前比较可信的解释，并诚实说明哪些还不确定。至少用一个动名词作主语的句子和一个 unless 句子。
